enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (40 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organization (12 marks); Expression (16 marks); Accuracy (12 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write on from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. You should write between 450 - 500 words. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity.

questions.enonce_markdown: **a)** Tell a story that ends with ... That was when peace finally returned to our family.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: a happy home spoiled by a quarrel over my late grandfather's land.
2. Build-up: Uncle Tabe claims the land, Father refuses, the two brothers stop speaking.
3. Climax: a fire at Uncle's farm, and Father is the first to run to help.
4. Resolution: the brothers embrace, the elders share the land, and the story ends with the required sentence.

**Model composition (487 words)**

Our family once lived in the village of Bokwai, and for many years our compound was the happiest place I knew. Every Sunday, my father, my uncle and their wives gathered under the mango tree to eat, laugh and tell stories. Then my grandfather died, and everything changed.

My grandfather left behind a large piece of land at the edge of the village, but he had not said clearly which of his sons should own it. My uncle Tabe, the elder, insisted that the land belonged to him by tradition. My father, who had farmed it for ten years, replied that he had earned it with his sweat. Their voices grew louder each day, and soon the Sunday meals stopped. The two brothers passed each other on the road without a greeting, and my cousins and I were forbidden to play together.

The quarrel soon spread to the whole village. Neighbours took sides, rumours flew from house to house, and my mother cried quietly in the kitchen at night. I was only twelve, but I understood that something precious was breaking. Whenever I asked my father why he would not talk to his brother, he simply answered, "Go and do your homework."

Months passed in this bitter silence. Then, one dry afternoon in January, I heard a frightening cry from the direction of my uncle's farm. "Fire! Fire!" the villagers shouted. The harmattan wind was carrying the flames across the dry grass toward his cocoa trees and his little house. Everybody ran out with buckets and branches, but the fire was spreading fast.

My father did not hesitate for one second. He dropped his machete, ran faster than I had ever seen him run and began beating the flames beside the men. His shirt was torn, his hands were burnt and his face was black with smoke, yet he refused to stop until the last flame had died. Uncle Tabe, who had been standing helplessly with tears in his eyes, looked at him in amazement. "After all I said about you?" he whispered.

"You are my brother," my father answered simply. "Land can be shared, but a brother cannot be replaced."

Uncle Tabe fell on his knees, took my father's blackened hands and begged for forgiveness. The two men embraced in front of the whole village, and many of the elders wiped their eyes. Within a week, the family council met under the mango tree. The elders divided the land into two equal parts, and each brother accepted his share gladly. My uncle even offered to help my father rebuild the fence that the fire had damaged.

On the following Sunday, the whole family sat together again under the mango tree, eating, laughing and telling stories just as before. I looked at my father and my uncle sharing a plate of roasted plantains, and my heart was full. That was when peace finally returned to our family.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organization | 12 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 16 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 12 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Not ending the story with the exact sentence required by the topic.
2. Telling a story with no build-up or clear problem, so that the ending (the return of peace) has no meaning.
